hook.text: Spray a field with glyphosate — everything dies except the Roundup Ready crop. Weed control simplified.

buildup.text: The EPSPS gene from Agrobacterium resists glyphosate — inserted into soy, corn, canola, and cotton.

discovery.text: No-till farming became possible — herbicide-tolerant crops let farmers skip plowing, reducing soil erosion by 90%.

twist.text: Overreliance created superweeds — Palmer amaranth evolved glyphosate resistance and now infests millions of acres.

climax.text: Stacked traits combine multiple herbicide tolerances — rotating chemistries slows resistance evolution.

punchline.text: Kill the weeds, save the crop — but evolution always fights back.

quiz.question: What unintended consequence arose from widespread Roundup Ready crop adoption?
options: Crop yields decreased due to the inserted gene
Weeds evolved glyphosate resistance, creating superweeds
The herbicide contaminated all groundwater permanently

details.summary: Herbicide-tolerant crops are engineered to survive specific herbicides that kill weeds, allowing farmers to spray fields without damaging crops. The most widespread example is Roundup Ready crops tolerant to glyphosate, grown on hundreds of millions of hectares.
details.whyItMatters: Herbicide tolerance simplified weed management and enabled no-till farming that reduces soil erosion. However, overreliance on single herbicides has driven the evolution of resistant superweeds, highlighting the need for diversified approaches.
takeaways: HT crops survive herbicide applications that kill surrounding weeds
Roundup Ready crops dominate soybean, corn, and cotton production
Herbicide-resistant weeds are increasing due to overreliance on glyphosate

faq.question: How do herbicide-tolerant crops survive being sprayed?
faq.answer: Most contain a modified version of the enzyme targeted by the herbicide. In Roundup Ready crops, a bacterial EPSPS enzyme replaces the plant's version, functioning normally even when glyphosate is present. The crop continues growing while weeds die.

faq.question: What is the superweed problem with HT crops?
faq.answer: Repeated use of the same herbicide selects for naturally resistant weed individuals. Over 50 weed species now resist glyphosate. Farmers must use additional herbicides or alternative strategies, partially negating the simplicity that HT crops originally provided.
